about: Eleven texts from an essay on romance by Joel (first person). Each is a passage just rewritten so it makes sense and follows (sometimes with the paragraph before or after it, unchanged, so the check has 50 words). Read each text as it stands, with its section heading and what the rewritten passage is for.

texts.heading: What we mean by “love” ❤️
texts.problem_fixed: Stumble: "the conflict starts to fall apart" skips a step; "But the horror is unavoidable" rebuts something unsaid.
sentences: Most people fail this test: what would I want if she herself thought she’d be happier with somebody else?
The first reaction is horror, but if they can get past it, wanting her and wanting her to be happy stop fighting each other.
Being wanted is part of what makes me want someone, so if she’d be happier with somebody else, I’d want her less anyway.
I still have to go through that horror, because I can’t wait until I know I’m wanted before I let her know I want her, and if we both do that, nothing gets started.
Once we’re together I still can’t wait to be sure.
If I start feeling less wanted, I may pull back, and she feels me pulling back and starts feeling less wanted herself, so she pulls back too.

texts.heading: It always goes deeper
texts.problem_fixed: Model one-line summary: "is not the same question as what makes me loved"; "in that particular way" vague.
sentences: Some women are fixer types, which can create the opposite pattern.
Before me, Bee had housed and supported a boyfriend who was totally broke and crazy, for a while.
Later she blamed herself for staying through that, and I agree, it wasn't appropriate.
It's not the same as helping carry somebody through a temporary incapacity, like she did with my knee.
What I still want to know is whether she’ll love me through a stretch when I can’t be what made me desirable, like with my knee.

texts.heading: Slow & steady isn’t KO’d yet
texts.problem_fixed: Model recap: four clipped lines restate B191; "Sex itself tells you other things" vague.
sentences: Women are always demanding to know why I love them.
Apparently they’re allowed not to know.
Those double-standards really bug me, but I also understand our brains work differently.
So that’s another thing to learn about over time in a relationship, and it sometimes hits you unexpectedly.
So go slowly if you can and learn what you can about each other before sex, but there are things you’ll only find out once you’re having it, like how your bodies respond to each other.

texts.heading: Don’t make your partner your whole world
texts.problem_fixed: Model listicle: six-item inventory "close friends, outside therapy..., and the ability to be alone"; friends repeats B218-B219.
sentences: You don’t need to spend as much time with friends as you did before the romance.
But keep some room to explore life on your own.
For me, that room is where I keep a mission of my own, separate interests and some connection to community.
I also get outside therapy when I need it, and I make sure I can still be alone.

texts.heading: Different levels in different domains can be complementary
texts.problem_fixed: Stumble: "Asking the question out loud" names no question, "where it starts" loose; three "maybe" clauses.
sentences: When we stop taking turns and one partner has become the default caregiver, and that’s taken for granted, it’s time to bring in other support, or the romance could collapse under the burden.
Then ask each other out loud whether the romance actually needs less intensity, should become a friendship, or should end.
I can’t answer that for others (and couldn’t always answer it for myself), but asking it is usually the first step.

texts.heading: Attraction and exclusivity
texts.problem_fixed: Stumble: "this ironically bureaucratic basis of romance" unclear; bonobo sentence doesn't connect to the first.
sentences: Ironically, sexclusivity, which we treat as the basis of romance, started out as that kind of bureaucratic record-keeping, and by the 17th century, when England began mass urbanization by forcing peasants off their land, it became the legal definition of marriage.

As for what comes naturally to us underneath that law, I’m not trying to say we’re just like bonobos, but the academic consensus is that humans tend toward flexible pair-bonding, with a propensity for occasional infidelity.

texts.heading: What will honesty produce?
texts.problem_fixed: Stumble: "If the other person won’t look" doesn't follow the Bee story; "It is its own reward" cliché.
sentences: Many people ask this question of honesty, but it’s unfair, because honesty is worth having whatever it leads to, and it can lead to very different places.
It might repair the relationship, open it, turn the romance into friendship, preserve the family through separation, or show you that ending it is better.
With Bee and me, it led to a temporary separation, which helped us, and that separation then became more permanent, although I’ve always thought maybe we would get back together in a few decades.
Any of those outcomes takes both of you, though, so if the other person won’t look at the truth with you, you can’t make it mutual, and then you have to decide what you can live with.

texts.heading: Psychedelic Timing
texts.problem_fixed: Model: "Advance planning doesn’t turn..." rebuts nothing said; "sober caveats may sound ridiculous" duplicates B415.
sentences: I’m putting the warning before anything good I say about psychedelics for relationships, because people need to hear it before they take anything.
I don’t think sexual consent should be negotiated for the first time while high, when the drug is changing how safe, loving, open, and connected everything feels.
And even if the two of you plan it all in advance, getting high and starting a relationship is still a risk.

texts.heading: Ending consciously
texts.problem_fixed: Model one-line thesis; B454-B455 answer only "whether", so "how to leave" hangs.
sentences: Before you think about how to leave, settle whether you’re leaving, and whether counseling is worth trying first.
You don’t owe it to them to try counseling unless you also owe it to yourself.
If you actually don’t want a good relationship with them anymore, go.
No amount of counseling will fix something that has nothing at the base of it.

texts.heading: What I gained from loss
texts.problem_fixed: Model: one point said three times ("only by the result", "process of growth", "not only whether you stayed").
sentences: From H., I learned that I can be extremely close to someone and feel completely understood and supported without actually falling in love.
I still treasure the support we gave/give each other.
Too many people judge a relationship only by whether they stayed together, when relationships are a process of growth in many dimensions, so start measuring what you actually learned from yours.

texts.heading: Tough Love
texts.problem_fixed: Model: opaque "myths... become real because we co-create them", four parallel myths; marriages joke is his.
sentences: We’re the ones who make the myths around romantic love real, by living as if they were true.
We act as though jealousy proves love and as though a permanent feeling can be promised, we keep our conflicts hidden, and when a relationship ends we call it a failure.
Those ideas were never natural laws, yet we suffer inside them, and we walk blindly into our first, second, third, fourth, and fifth marriages!
